topic: planning and scheduling an overnight sourdough bake in a small bakery

provenance.author: subagent-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is batch arithmetic on the same bake with closed task questions, base is a diagnostic conversation about a late finish. Grounded external referent: the proving cabinet, introduced in turn 0 and carried through the whole diagnosis (it holds the tubs overnight, only takes four of them, and its setting is one of the two suspects).

a: Here are five doughs for tomorrow, and their flour weights need working through in order.
The country dough takes twelve kilograms and the rye takes six kilograms of flour.
The spelt takes four kilograms, and the seeded takes five kilograms on the same sheet.
The focaccia is the smallest of the five at three kilograms of flour.
Sort them from heaviest to lightest, and give the running total after each one.
How many kilograms of flour does the whole bake come to in the end?
base: Our overnight bake keeps drifting late, and the last two racks leave the oven after the shop opens.
We mix at four in the afternoon and load the proving cabinet an hour later.
The cabinet takes only four tubs, so the rye always stands out on the bench beside it.
The rye is the one holding everything up, even though it is the smallest batch we make.
Where would you start looking for the hour we keep losing somewhere in that long stretch?

a: Sorted heaviest to lightest, the order runs country then rye then seeded then spelt then focaccia.
The running totals after each dough are twelve then eighteen then twenty-three kilograms of flour.
The last two totals are twenty-seven and then thirty kilograms of flour.
Water at seventy-eight percent gives the country dough nine thousand three hundred sixty grams.
The rye takes four thousand six hundred eighty grams of water at that hydration.
Does the total flour of thirty kilograms match the figure on the order sheet?
base: The cabinet is the first thing I would measure, because its shelves rarely sit at one temperature.
Rye acidifies fast but rises slowly when it is chilled, so it looks sluggish for hours.
Standing outside the cabinet on a fifteen degree bench will stretch that rye bulk badly.
I would want the actual dough temperature after mixing, not the reading on the cabinet dial.
Do you take any temperature at all when the doughs go in for the night?

a: Now add the levain at twenty percent of each dough's own flour weight.
List the levain weight for all five doughs in the heaviest to lightest order.
Salt goes in at two percent of flour, rounded to the nearest five grams.
Put the three wheat doughs in bin one, and the rye and focaccia in bin two.
Which levain weight belongs to the seeded dough at that fixed percentage?
base: We measure nothing after mixing and we never look at the cabinet dial either.
The cabinet sits on the far wall and it has run at the same setting for years.
The mixer runs eight minutes on second speed and the room is near twenty degrees then.
By midnight the shutters are down and the rye tub by the door drops several degrees more.
Would moving that tub into the cabinet be enough on its own?

a: The country dough takes two thousand four hundred grams of levain at twenty percent.
The rye takes one thousand two hundred grams, and the seeded takes one thousand grams.
The spelt takes eight hundred grams and the focaccia takes six hundred grams of levain.
Bin one holds country salt of two hundred forty grams, with seeded at one hundred grams.
Bin two holds rye salt of one hundred twenty grams and focaccia salt of sixty grams.
Does the levain total of six thousand grams agree with the bin sheet?
base: Moving the rye into the cabinet would help, though it may swing the other way in summer.
What you want is a steady twenty-two degrees rather than the warmest corner in the room.
I would also shorten the rye bulk and let it finish its proof in the tin.
Rye rarely rewards a long bulk and it does better with a short one.
How firm is the rye when you scale it, and does it hold its shape on the cabinet shelf?

a: One correction before we go further: the seeded dough is five and a half kilograms.
Recalculate its water, its levain and its salt, and leave the other four untouched.
Then give the new totals for flour and for water across the whole bake.
After that list the five doughs in the order they enter the oven tomorrow.
Which dough goes in first under the order rye then country then spelt then seeded?
base: The rye scales soft and it spreads on the bench within a minute of shaping.
We use eighty-five percent hydration on it, which is what the old recipe card says.
Nobody has changed that number in years, and the cabinet has run the same way just as long.
The bags look the same but the loaves have been flatter since about November.
Could a different rye flour really cost us a whole hour of proofing time?

a: The seeded dough at five and a half kilograms takes four thousand two hundred ninety grams of water.
Its levain becomes one thousand one hundred grams, and its salt one hundred ten grams.
The new flour total is thirty and a half kilograms across the whole bake.
The new water total comes to twenty-three thousand seven hundred ninety grams.
Does the oven order still begin with the rye batch as it was set out?
base: A flour change can absolutely cost an hour, especially with rye and its damaged starch.
New crop or a different mill will drink water differently at the same stated hydration.
I would drop the rye to seventy-eight percent and see whether it holds a shape better.
Then keep the bulk short and give the tins a longer proof in the cabinet.
Do you still have a few kilos of the old flour to run a proper comparison?

a: Convert the whole bake into bags of flour at twenty-five kilograms to the bag.
Tell me how many full bags that needs and what remains in the open bag.
Then split the total water into two vessels of equal volume, and give each figure.
The oven schedule starts at five in the morning, with loads twenty-five minutes apart.
How many full bags does thirty and a half kilograms of flour come to?
base: There are two sacks of the old flour left in the store room, maybe forty kilos.
We could bake both versions on the same night if the schedule allows a second mix.
The cabinet shelf takes four tubs, though, and the country doughs are already divided by then.
Two rye tubs side by side would mean stacking, and stacked tubs run warmer inside.
Is a stacked tub going to spoil the comparison we are trying to make here?

a: Thirty and a half kilograms is one full bag plus five and a half kilograms.
Each of the two vessels holds eleven thousand eight hundred ninety-five grams of water.
The rye goes into the oven at five, and the country at five twenty-five.
The spelt goes in at five fifty and the seeded at six fifteen.
The focaccia goes in at six forty, closing an oven window of one hour forty minutes.
base: Stacked tubs will spoil it, since the middle of a stack can sit two degrees warmer.
Put them side by side on the cabinet shelf and swap their positions halfway through.
Better still, halve both batches so each one fits a single tub on the shelf.
Scale, shape and tin them within the same ten minutes so nothing else differs.
Record dough temperature at mix, at the end of bulk and before the tins go in.

a: Print a short checklist of the four steps in order for the night crew.
Step one is mixing, step two is bulk and step three is shaping.
Step four is proofing, and each step needs the clock time for the rye batch.
Mixing begins at four in the afternoon and the tins go in at five.
Which clock time closes the bulk if the bulk runs for thirty minutes?
base: That sounds workable, and halving both batches costs us nothing but two extra tins.
I will write the cabinet readings on the tub lids so the night crew records them.
One worry is the seeded dough, which shares the bench and the same shaping window.
If the rye takes longer to shape, the seeded loaves will sit around waiting.
Should the seeded batch go into the cold room while the rye is being handled?

a: Step one is the mix at sixteen hundred, and it runs eight minutes on second speed.
Step two is the bulk from sixteen ten until sixteen forty as instructed.
Step three is the scaling and shaping between sixteen forty and sixteen fifty-five.
Step four is the proof from sixteen fifty-five until five in the morning, roughly twelve hours.
The tins go into the oven at five, and that order holds for the whole night.
base: Yes, park the seeded tub in the cold room for the twenty minutes the rye needs.
Cold slows it enough that it will hold while the bench is busy with rye.
Bring it back out just before shaping so the surface does not skin over.
Then it goes onto the cabinet shelf with the rest and the lids get the times.
Two nights of that and the flour puzzle should settle itself from the notes alone.
